system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 8 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 60-85 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2179-06-16 11:22:00 to 2179-06-23 21:55:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A male patient, 21 days post orthotopic liver transplant for cryptogenic cirrhosis, was readmitted with fever, hypotension, and worsening back and abdominal pain. Imaging revealed left upper lobe ground-glass opacities consistent with early pneumonia and a large subphrenic fluid collection. He was started on Vancomycin and Cefepime based on prior Enterococcus bacteremia. A cervical spine MRI ruled out spinal infection, showing only degenerative changes. A PICC line was placed to complete intravenous antibiotic therapy at an extended care facility. His condition improved with treatment, inflammatory markers decreased, and he regained mobility with minimal assistance. He was discharged back to rehabilitation with plans for continued IV antibiotics, tube feeds, and close monitoring of transplant and metabolic parameters.
problems: Diaphragmatic hernia without mention of obstruction or gangrene
Personal history of malignant neoplasm of prostate

INDICATION:  ___ man with elevated LFTs, mark the spot for liver
biopsy.

FINDINGS:  With the patient in end expiration and the right arm over the head,
a mark was made over the right lobe of the liver at the mid axillary line for
a biopsy to be performed by the clinical staff.

IMPRESSION:  Right lobe of the liver marked for biopsy to be performed by the
clinical staff.

AP CHEST, 2:41 P.M. ___  

HISTORY:  Assess PIC line.

IMPRESSION:  AP chest compared to ___:

Right PIC line extends as far as the low SVC.  Feeding tube is coiled in the
stomach and passes out of view.  Heart size top normal unchanged.  Band of
atelectasis at the base of the right lung are unchanged is the only focal
pulmonary abnormality.  No appreciable pleural effusion or evidence of central
adenopathy.  No pneumothorax.

HISTORY:  Patient with cirrhosis, elevated LFTs and altered mental status;
rule acute intracranial pathology.

TECHNIQUE:  Multiplanar and multisequence MRI of the brain was performed
without intravenous contrast. According to the technologist's note scanned
into PACS, contrast could not be administered as the patient was not able to
remain still during the examination or complete the examination due to "severe
pain."

FINDINGS: There is no relevant prior imaging for comparison.

There is no acute intracranial infarct or hemorrhage. There is extensive,
confluent FLAIR- and T2-hyperintensity in subcortical and white matter,
representing the sequelae of chronic small vessel ischemic disease.  Similar
changes are also seen in the brainstem.  There is generalized volume loss of
the brain parenchyma.  There is no evidence of mass, mass effect, edema or
shift of normal midline structures.  

The paranasal sinuses are clear.  There is no abnormality of regional bone
marrow signal.

IMPRESSION: Limited (non-enhanced) study with no evidence of an acute
intracranial process, global atrophy and sequelae of chronic small vessel
ischemic disease.

HISTORY:  Patient with cirrhosis, elevated LFTs and tremor; rule out cervical
abnormality.

TECHNIQUE:  Sagittal T1- and T2-weighted images of the cervical spine, only,
were obtained without intravenous contrast; axial sequences could not be
obtained. According to the technologist's note scanned into PACS, contrast
could not be administered, as the patient was not able to remain still during
the examination or complete the study, due to "severe pain."

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, Mr. Johnson. I'm Dr. Patel, one of your transplant team doctors. I understand you came in because your liver tests were high and you’ve been having some tremors.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s right. My wife noticed my hands shaking more than usual yesterday. And I’ve had some headaches too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You mentioned the tremors have been going on for a few weeks, but got worse recently?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, subtle at first—just a little shaky when I ate. But yesterday, my head started moving too, and I had trouble finding words for a moment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That sounds concerning. We’ll need to check a few things. You’re here for a liver biopsy today, which was planned because of the elevated liver enzymes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Right. They marked my side earlier this morning. Is it safe? I’m a bit nervous.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a routine procedure. We use imaging to guide the needle, and we’ll monitor your blood afterward to make sure there’s no bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, good. My appetite’s been poor lately. And the feeding tube got clogged a couple nights ago.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see that in your chart. We’ll keep an eye on your nutrition. For now, we’ll hold off on tube feeds since you’re able to eat a little.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The biopsy went well. No complications. We’ll get the results in a day or two.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks, doctor. I’ve been feeling a bit weak. Is that normal after the biopsy?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Some fatigue is expected. We’ll keep you lying on your side for a few hours to reduce any risk of bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked a chest X-ray to make sure your PICC line is in the right place. It is—good news.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s one less thing to worry about. What about the tremors? Could they be from the transplant meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Tacrolimus can cause tremors, but the new movements you’re describing—head shaking, facial grimacing—make us want to look further.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what’s next?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve ordered an MRI of your head and cervical spine to rule out any structural issues. Given your pain, we may not be able to do the full study, but we’ll try.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The head MRI is back. No stroke or bleeding. But there’s some chronic small vessel disease and brain atrophy—common with age and your history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that why I’m having tremors?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not likely. Those changes don’t explain the sudden movements. The cervical MRI showed arthritis in your neck, but no spinal cord compression.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what’s causing it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re not sure yet. A neurologist is reviewing your case. We’re also checking your potassium—it was high earlier.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: High potassium? I didn’t know that could affect movement.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can cause muscle weakness or irregular heartbeats, but not typically tremors. Still, we’re treating it with medication to bring it down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The liver ultrasound shows no bile duct blockage, but we’re still concerned. We’re scheduling an ERCP to look directly at the bile ducts.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Another procedure? What’s an ERCP?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a scope passed through your mouth to the liver area. We can see the bile ducts and fix any narrow spots.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I be asleep?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’ll be sedated. We’ll remove the feeding tube temporarily for the procedure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The ERCP went well. We found a narrow spot at the bile duct connection. We opened it and placed two stents to keep it open.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. This should help your liver numbers improve. Your enzymes are already trending down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the tremors?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They’ve improved since yesterday. The neurologist thinks they may not be from a physical cause. Stress or anxiety could be playing a role.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been stressed, sure. But it felt real.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It was real. But sometimes the body expresses emotional strain through physical symptoms. We’ve involved social work to help with family stress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your potassium is still high. We’ve started Florinef and low-dose Lasix to help your kidneys manage it better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need these long-term?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll see. It may improve as your liver function stabilizes. We’ll monitor closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been having right upper belly pain with eating. We did an EGD—just mild stomach irritation, nothing serious.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So why does it hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly from bile flow changes or your hiatal hernia. We’ve switched you to a stronger stomach protector—lansoprazole.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your tremors haven’t returned. That’s a good sign. The neuro team feels it’s safe to cancel the lumbar MRI.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I couldn’t have stayed still anyway—my back hurts too much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We don’t want to put you through unnecessary pain. Your liver tests are improving thanks to the stents.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked another scan to make sure the stents haven’t moved. They’re in place—great news.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’m healing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Your liver numbers are going down, potassium is better, and you’re eating well. We’re thinking about discharge soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The transplant team evaluated you. You’re stable and safe to go home. We’ll set up visiting nurses and labs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll need help with meds, though. My wife and daughter can assist.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll do a full med teaching session. You’re on tacrolimus, prednisone, and insulin—same as before, with a few changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Like what?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll start ursodiol for bile flow, mirtazapine for sleep and appetite, and fludrocortisone for potassium control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the tremors—what if they come back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call us immediately if you have dizziness, confusion, or shaking. But we’re hopeful it won’t return.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today’s the day. You’re doing well—walking on your own, eating, and stable vitals.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready to go home. Thanks for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Remember: labs tomorrow, then weekly. Take your meds as shown, and call if you feel worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And thank the nurses too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’ll pass that along. Take care, Mr. Johnson. We’ll see you in clinic soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—should I avoid lifting?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, nothing over 10 pounds for now. And no driving until your next appointment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re all set. The discharge papers are ready, and your family can bring the car around.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad this is behind me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve made great progress. Keep following up, and take it one day at a time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. See you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care, Mr. Johnson.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One last question—what about my headaches?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They’re likely tension-type, related to stress. The mirtazapine should help with sleep and reduce them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll give it a try.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good plan. And keep using the antacid as needed for stomach discomfort.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re all set. We’ll be in touch after your first lab results.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks, doctor. Really appreciate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care of yourself and keep in touch.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. See you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Goodbye, Mr. Johnson.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Bye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will help you get ready to leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Have a good day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: You too.

summary.summary_paragraph: A male patient, status post orthotopic liver transplant, was admitted for evaluation of elevated liver enzymes and new-onset tremors. A liver biopsy was performed, which ruled out rejection but showed neutrophilic inflammation. An ERCP revealed a biliary stricture at the anastomosis, which was treated with sphincterotomy and placement of two biliary stents. His liver function tests subsequently improved. He developed hyperkalemia, managed with kayexalate, fludrocortisone, and low-dose furosemide. Neurological evaluation for abnormal involuntary movements, including head shaking and facial grimacing, found no acute intracranial or spinal cord abnormalities on MRI; the movements resolved, and a psychological component was considered. An EGD showed only mild gastropathy. The patient stabilized, resumed oral intake, and was discharged home with family support, visiting nurse services, and a plan for weekly lab monitoring.
